1. CSCase.com

CSCase․com is a third-party website where users can open CS2/CS:GO cases․ One free case is available on the site and can be opened without a deposit․ Free openings help attract new users by allowing them to win prizes without paying (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a)․ CSCase․com and CaseDrop․eu are not affiliated with Valve or the Steam platform‚ but they use the Steam market to distribute prizes‚ just as other sites in this category do (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a; Revolvertech‚ 2026)․

At the time of our review‚ CSCase․com had an average Trustpilot rating of 4․4 stars out of 5 from 404 reviews‚ a higher average rating than other websites of this type but also reviews of major issues described below (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a)․
2․ Description and link to gambling activity

CSCase․com‌ works similarly to CaseDrop․eu and other case-opening websites․ Users pay real money to open virtual cases‌ and receive random skins․ Users can potentially sell their virtual skins‌ on other websites and marketplaces and transfer the proceeds to their Steam accounts for real money (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a; CS․Money‚ n․d․)․ A Trustpilot review of CSCase․com mentions a "13%‌ bonus on deposit" promotion for new users․ Other gambling sites‌ offer similar deposit-matching promotions to attract deposits (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a)․

A common complaint in reviews is that "top-tier" (expensive) cases contain the lowest-rarity skins in their prize pool‚ as also noted in other reviews about games of this type (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a; Steamanalyst‚ 2026‚ reviews previously cited‌ for CaseDrop․eu)․ These findings echo other reviews stating that most prize items awarded for play‌ in this and other types of games have low value compared to the cost of playing (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a; Steamanalyst‚ 2026)․ These findings also align with research on prize items for CS2 cases‚‌ which indicates that about 80% of CS2 case openings result in the lowest-rarity prize (Steamanalyst‚ 2026)․

Gambling Risk: High and Direct․ Users can deposit cash and bet on the outcome of a random event like a court case․ They can then withdraw cash through the same two-step process used to sell other items on this platform to third-party websites (CS․Money‚ n․d․; SellYourSkins‚ 2026)․
3․ Age and Risk of Addiction Problems

No age verification (KYC) practices were noted for CSCase․com in available sources․ Offering a free‚ no-deposit required case as part of the onboarding process may pose risks‚ as it allows new users to interact with the site at no cost‚ potentially broadening the site's audience to include younger or more reckless users before they make a deposit (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a)․ This is consistent with the findings of the UK regulatory review of unlicensed skin gambling sites referenced in your own project‚ which found that 11- to 14-year-olds were more likely to use these sites than adults (Harris‚ Griffiths & Gibson‚ 2025)․
4․ Risk or Danger
Risk Level: High‚ 7/10

The most well-documented risk is a refusal to allow withdrawals when shopping has been profitable․ One review describes opening at least 4‚000 low-cost accounts and making a profit‚ then having withdrawal requests denied for "fraud activity‚" which this reviewer describes as a convenient excuse with little evidence (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a)․ Another review describes having items on order and being unable to withdraw them‚ with customer service representatives failing to answer further questions from the reviewer (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a)․ These are customer complaints and should be viewed as anecdotal evidence‚ not firm evidence of company policies‚ but they are similar in nature to the documented withdrawal problems at CaseDrop․eu and other sites in this category‚ with similar complaints posted for csgocases․com‚ CSGO․net‚ CS2Land‚ and GGdrop during this review (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-b‚ n․d․-c‚ n․d․-d‚ n․d․-e)․

This broader trend should be noted in your company's documentation about your business model: Challenges related to withdrawals following a successful opening are common among other online companies offering similar CS2 skin-opening services and have been reported by users of multiple other unlicensed CS2 skin-opening services․ These reports suggest that withdrawal difficulties following a successful opening are a risk of operating unlicensed CS2 skin-opening services in general‚ not just a problem with one particular service (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a‚ n․d․-b‚ n․d․-c‚ n․d․-d‚ n․d․-e)․

Another risk is the same reliance on Steam trading services mentioned earlier with respect to CaseDrop․eu: trade holds‚ restrictions on bot account trading activity‚ and the need to stock inventory of actual skins to pay out winners‚ all of which cannot be confirmed by users before using the service (Revolvertech‚ 2026)․

A third potential drawback is that higher-priced products have poor payout ratios‚ as other commenters have said above․ If this claim is true‚ it suggests that the platform offers lower payouts for its higher-priced products‚ which could increase financial risks for users who choose these products (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a)․

A fourth risk shared by all sites in this category and previously discussed in connection with CaseDrop․eu is the lack of licensing in any country or territory‚ and CSCase․com falls into the same "unlicensed skins gambling site" category explored in a study commissioned by the government of the United Kingdom (Harris‚ Griffiths‚ & Gibson‚ 2025)․
5․ Tier Classification
Tier: T6‚ Unlicensed real-money gambling (main)‚ plus T3-like gray-market payout service‚ similar to CaseDrop․eu‚ as an intermediary step․

The deposit side of the model is straightforward‚ users actually pay money to the service provider to bet on a specific outcome in a legal case․ The betting service provider has not been licensed in any jurisdictions covered by these reviews (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a)․ This model is the same as T6 described elsewhere in this taxonomy․

The cash-out process for prizes involves two transactions‚ including one on Steam and another on a third-party platform‚ similar to pattern T3 (Grey-market Convertible) and the process used by CaseDrop․eu (CS․Money‚ n․d․; SellYourSkins‚ 2026)․
Classification path:

CSCase․com → Depositor pays with real money → Random entry into paid case-opening contests or free no-deposit contests → Gratuity in the form of skins if deposited money can be withdrawn → Steam account → Sale of skins on third-party websites → Cash → T6 account with T3 overlay

Taxonomy note: CSCase․com and CaseDrop․eu should be listed separately but within a single class in your taxonomy proposal․ Although CSCase․com and CaseDrop․eu have the same basic scoring and ranking approach‚ they are operated by different companies and have other distinguishing factors‚ including deposit bonuses and free cases for new customers‚ as well as different customer complaints about withdrawals․ Taxonomy guidance: Your team could use the CSCase․com and CaseDrop․eu examples to evaluate other websites in the "skin-trading and skin-betting ecosystems" class mentioned in your Scope section․ Other websites in this class would also be listed separately but within a single class and would have the same basic scoring and ranking approach․
6․ Financial Score
Financial Score: 7/10‚ High

CSCase․com offers the same no-deposit staking model as CaseDrop․eu‚ including an economic incentive structure similar to a house edge‚ based on user reports of lower success rates for more expensive stakes on both sites (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a)․ CSCase․com's user rating is slightly lower than CaseDrop․eu's 8/10 rating‚ partly due to the no-deposit option‚ which lets users try the site without risking money․ Section 3 discusses other risks related to this feature․
7․ Monetary Value
Monetary Outcomes: Potential to earn money and sell the product or service in a secondary market‚ assuming the opportunity to sell exists․

The money route is similar to CaseDrop․eu's: real cash → case-opening wager → random assignment of skins → withdrawal from Steam inventory (subject to approval) → sale on another website → real cash (CS․Money‚ n․d․)․

Monetary Value Rating: 7/10‚ one point lower than CaseDrop․eu's 8/10‚ due to reports of complaints about being unable to withdraw funds from CSCase․com‚ among other issues‚ which may prevent some users from successfully cashing out (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a)․

Unofficial CS2 skin gambling site offering case opening, case battles, and casino-style games (Roulette, Crash, Coinflip, Mines, Plinko, Towers, Wheel, Jackpot) plus esports betting
Primary Audience
CS2/CS:GO players; operating since 2021, self-categorised as a "Gambling Service"
Gambling Connection
Direct — self-identifies as a gambling service; offers explicit casino game formats, not just loot-box case opening
Addiction / Harm Score
9/10 – Very High
Risk Score
9/10 – Very High
Tier Classification
T6 – Unlicensed Real-money Wagering (primary), with a T3-style grey-market conversion step for skin/crypto payouts
Financial Score
8/10 – High
Monetary Value
Real money/crypto/skins in → casino-style or case-opening wager → skin or crypto payout → convertible to cash externally
Regulatory Status

1. CSGOLuck.com

CSGOLuck․com is a CS2 skin gambling site that has operated since 2021 and lists its company type on Trustpilot as "Gambling Service" (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a)․ CSGOLuck differs from other sites like CaseDrop․eu and CSCase․com in its focus on skin gambling․ In addition to case opening‚ CSGOLuck provides other gambling services‚ including Case Battles‚ Crash‚ Roulette‚ Coinflip‚ Mines‚ Plinko‚ Towers‚ Wheel‚ Jackpot‚ and esports betting added in 2024 (Fairness․gg‚ 2026; Coincasinohub‚ 2026)․ These features make CSGOLuck more similar to an online casino than other skin gambling sites‚ it offers games like Crash‚ Roulette‚ and Mines that are common casino games with a skin gambling twist‚ rather than games that simulate skin collections․

An independent review of the site's terms of service and AML/KYC pages found no mention of a gambling license on the site (CSDB․gg‚ 2026)․ A second review identified the site's operator as GG Technologies Limited‚ Belize company registration number 000033728 (CS2Pulse‚ 2026)․ A third review supporting the lack of regulation at the site notes‚ "CSGOLuck's terms of service do not identify a regulating body‚" as well as reports from third parties about the Belize-registered operator (CSGamblingSite‚ 2026)․
2․ Description and Gambling-Related Use

CSGOLuck offers‌ deposit methods including cryptocurrencies and CS2 skins‚ as well as Visa and Mastercard credit‌ and debit cards․ Prize payouts are‌ limited to CS2 skins and cryptocurrencies and cannot be made in‌ cash․ Methods for converting‌ prize‌ earnings to cash include selling CS2 skins on other marketplaces and trading cryptocurrencies on exchanges‚ similar processes used by CaseDrop․eu and CSCase․com (Freeskinshub‚ 2026)․ Fairness․gg‌ (2026)․

Unlike CSCase․com and CaseDrop․eu‚‌ CSGOLuck requires identity verification for withdrawal of‌ cryptocurrencies and skins and for other services‚ including live chat‚ on Freeskinshub (2026)․ At first glance‚ this policy‌ seems‌ to offer greater consumer protection than the no-KYC policies of the other two sites․ However‚ other reviews indicate‌ that CSGOLuck‌ uses the KYC requirement to block payments to consumers․ For example‚ one‌ review says‚ "Scam site‚ keep asking for extra KYC and then refuse to send the money back‚" and another review says the reviewer deposited funds and won over $400 while playing on the site but was then unable to complete the verification process‚ had the account closed‚ and did not receive a refund‌ (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-b)․ These experiences with‌ CSGOLuck differ from and may be‌ more problematic than the simple no-KYC issues faced by users of CSCase․com and CaseDrop․eu․

Gambling Link: Stronger and more open than links found on other sites listed in this classification․ CSGOLuck is the first site listed in this classification to identify itself as a "Gambling Service" on a review site‚ unlike other sites listed here that primarily market skin-collecting and purchasing services (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a)․
3․ Age and Risk of Substance Abuse or Addiction Issues

No age-verification process was found at sign-up for CSGOLuck․ Users must apply KYC procedures to withdraw funds but can deposit and play without age verification (Freeskinshub‚ 2026)․ Similar issues for underage users have been reported for CSCase․com and CaseDrop․eu in the context of the UK Department of Culture‚ Media and Sport review of online gambling sites offering skins (Harris‚ Griffiths & Gibson‚ 2025)․

Addiction/Harm Score: 9/10‚ Very High․ The highest Addiction/Harm Score among the three websites in this category profiled in this taxonomy․ Key factors contributing to this score include the availability of pure casino-style games (Crash‚ Mines‚ Coinflip‚ and Roulette) with no browsing or collection aspects; "daily cases system based on your level" and "rake back" player loyalty programs aimed at increasing player engagement; and multiple reports of large winners being blocked or banned after winning big‚ described in more detail in Section 4 (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a‚ n․d․-c)․ Like other profiles in this taxonomy‚ this profile is based on available information about the design and use of the websites and is not a clinical assessment․
4․ Risk or Danger
Risk Level: Very High‚ 9/10

The most significant user complaint against CSGOLuck‚ which explains why CSGOLuck has a lower reputation than CaseDrop․eu and CSCase․com‚ is a consistent issue involving account restrictions and bans following large wins but not other activity․ One user review reads‚ "I won big on slots (le ZEUS)‚ and they instantly restricted my withdraw‚ I tried to talk to them for more than 6 hours on live support‚ and when nothing worked‚ they banned me" (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a)․ This issue is more severe than other withdrawal issues because it affects only users who win large amounts․ If widespread‚ such problems suggest that CSGOLuck does not intend to pay out at advertised odds for large wins․

A second risk associated with KYC is use for denial purposes rather than protection‚ described in Section 2 of the report‚ including a Trustpilot (n․d․-b) report of a $400 or more account being shut down and refunds not being paid․

A third harm is the silencing of user complaints in other communication channels on the site․ One reviewer reports being "ghosted and muted for 24 hours‚ never responded" by platform staff on Discord and says that "many on chat and discord have complained of recent issues and withdraw struggles‚ just to have their messages deleted" (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a)․ Another reviewer states that chat moderators on the site deleted complainant messages regarding a seven-day delay in crediting deposited trade-locked skins (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-c)․ Active censorship of complaints on the site itself may prevent other users from learning about problems with the site before using it‚ a harm not mentioned by evidence on CaseDrop․eu or CSCase․com․

A fourth concern is the lack of a gambling license reference on the site‚ which two other evaluations explicitly reviewed on the site's terms and KYC/AML pages found (CSDB․gg‚ 2026; CSGamblingSite‚ 2026)․ CSGOLuck joins CaseDrop․eu and CSCase․com as unlicensed offshore gambling sites but offers casino-style games in addition to case games․

Important note for your team's investigation of CSGOLuck: The site also has many positive reviews (649-658 on Trustpilot with an average rating of 4 out of 5 stars) detailing customer experiences with easy deposits and withdrawals and successful KYC verification (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a)․ One review site notes that "Trustpilot has flagged CSGOLuck for potentially soliciting reviews outside its guidelines" and offers other information about CSGOLuck to help your team evaluate the credibility of these positive reviews (Fairness․gg‚ 2026)․ The negative reviews cited above suggest a pattern of complaints by users‚ though they do not prove that all users attempting to use the site are unable to get paid․ CSGOLuck has mixed evidence‚ unlike the all-negative reviews of CSCase․com․
5․ Tier Classification
Tier: T6‚ Illegal Real-money Gambling (primary)‚ including a T3-style grey-market conversion process to accept other forms of payment‚ such as skins or cryptocurrencies․

The deposit process is well documented․ Players can use cash or virtual currencies and skins as deposits on a site offering casino-style games from an unlicensed online casino‚ Freeskinshub and CSDB․gg are two examples․ This is similar to T6․ Documentation from these sites is clearer than that from CaseDrop․eu and CSCase․com because CSGOLuck offers Casino-style games‚ including Crash‚ Roulette‚ and Mines‚ in addition to loot boxes․

The spending side would involve at least one step outside the skin market‚ you would have to sell skins on other market sites and convert cryptocurrency if you wanted to use the proceeds to buy traditional goods․ This would be a type T3 (grey-market convertible) site like the other two skin market sites profiled here (Freeskinshub‚ 2026)․
Classification path:

CSGOLuck․com → cash or skin deposit → casino-style or case-opening bet (Crash‚ Roulette‚ Mines‚ Coinflip) → skins or cash prize‚ assuming withdrawal is successful → sale on another platform or exchange → cash → T6 with T3 conversion step

Taxonomy note: The CSGOLuck site provides evidence that "skin-trading and skin-betting ecosystems" should be considered a taxonomy dimension with multiple categories rather than a single category․ Similar sites‚ including CaseDrop․eu and CSCase․com‚ more closely resemble loot boxes with additional opportunities to cash out; CSGOLuck more closely resembles an unregulated online casino that uses skins and cryptocurrencies instead of traditional currencies․ You may wish to add a new taxonomy subcategory to differentiate sites offering only case-opening services from those offering casino games‚ as there are important regulatory and other differences between such sites․
6․ Financial Score
Financial Score: 8/10‚ High

CSGOLuck's offer of the Crash‚ Roulette‚ and Mines games‚ which are fast-paced‚ ongoing casino games‚ makes it more similar to licensed casinos offering Blackjack and Roulette‚ as described in other entries in this taxonomy‚ than to CaseDrop․eu and CSCase․com‚ which have a one-time cost associated with opening each case․ The CSGOLuck score is lower than the scores for licensed Blackjack and Roulette casinos‚ both of which are 9/10‚ because information about CSGOLuck's house edge could not be found and CSGOLuck does not have an estimated loss impact in Australia‚ while other sources provide an estimated loss impact for illegal gambling in Australia‚ as described in other entries (CSGamblingSite‚ 2026)․
7․ Monetary Value
Monetary Value: Players can purchase skins or other items with real money or cryptocurrency and sell them for skins or cryptocurrency‚ if the sale is allowed by the platform․

The financial route: Deposit real money or in-game currency․ Make an online gambling or case-purchase wager․ Win in-game currency or cryptocurrency․ Sell in-game currency or cryptocurrency on other platforms․ Cash out․ (Freeskinshub‚ 2026)

Monetary Value Rating: 7/10‚ lower than CaseDrop․eu's 8/10 rating‚ partly due to consistent reports and other evidence of past winners being disqualified or blocked from claiming high-value prizes‚ adding risk that high-value prize winners will fail to claim their prizes (Trustpilot‚ n․d․-a)․

Name
Pool. Representative title: 8 Ball Pool (Miniclip). Real-money variant: skill-cash pool apps
Candidate Class
Free-to-play competitive skill game with coin-staked matches and paid random boxes (proposed new candidate class; overlaps the paid loot-box and children's reward-token classes)
Primary Audience
Teenagers and young adults. The US App Store listing rates it 13+ and flags loot boxes and contests; the Australian listing shows 16+
Gambling Connection

Moderate / Indirect. Paid chance-based items and coin stakes, but no cash-out route identified for the main game; a 2019 review also reported simulated-gambling side games (Children and Media Australia, 2019)
Addiction / Harm Score
5/10: Moderate
Risk Score
5/10: Moderate
Tier Classification
T2: paid random draw, no cash-out (8 Ball Pool). Skill-cash pool apps: T4/T5 boundary
Financial Score
5/10: Moderate
Monetary Value
Closed-loop virtual currency (coins and cash) bought with real money; official sources identify no conversion to real money
Regulatory Status

8 Ball Pool: no gambling-regulator action found in the sources reviewed. The US listing is 13+ and the Australian listing 16+, both with loot-box and contest labels (Apple, n.d.-a; Apple, n.d.-b); compliance with Australia's minimum M rating for paid chance-based purchases is unchecked (Australian Classification Board, 2024). Skill-cash pool apps: legality rests on the skill-contest argument; they are prohibited in India since 1 May 2026 (Lexology, 2026; Press Information Bureau, 2026) and the Australian position is unverified.
1. Pool

8 Ball Pool is a free-to-play online pool game from Miniclip. Its core function is competitive pool, but it also runs Surprise Boxes, Scratch and Win scratchers, a Golden Spin, Golden Shot Tickets, and a Pool Pass (Apple, n.d.-b; Miniclip, n.d.). A separate real-money version exists on skill-contest platforms, where players pay an entry fee to win cash prizes (Skillz, n.d.).
2. Description and Connection to Gambling

8 Ball Pool is a free-to-play online pool game from Miniclip. Players can stake in-game currency on the outcome of head-to-head matches (Apple, n.d.-a). Coins and items also come from random "Surprise Boxes" whose contents and probabilities Miniclip publishes, with some top-tier cue pieces at 0.125% (Miniclip, n.d.). The US listing carries App Store labels for loot boxes and frequent contests (Apple, n.d.-a).

Unlike the material of the social-casino apps, there is no indication in the official material reviewed of how the coins can be converted into cash, and match results are based on skill rather than chance. The gambling link is the paid chance-based items (boxes, scratchers, spins), which research considers psychologically similar to gambling (Drummond & Sauer, 2018). There are also skill-cash pool apps; a commercial example is Skillz, which details in general terms how the system works: players pay to enter contests for cash prizes, with the results based on skill. However, the page was not checked for a specific pool title (Skillz, n.d.). According to a Children and Media Australia (2019) review, side games in the app included a spin wheel, a Scratch and Win feature, boxes, and a paid Hi-Lo guessing game, which were described as simulated gambling. The review advised against the app for children aged 15 and under. The review may no longer reflect the current app because it covered only one version, so the functionality of the current version should be verified.
Moderate / Indirect Gambling Connection: The buying behaviour is similar to gambling, while the outcome space of the main game is closed-loop.
3. Age Group and Addiction Risk

Primary age group: Teenagers and young adults. The US listing gives a 13+ rating and the Australian listing 16+ (Apple, n.d.-a; Apple, n.d.-b). Whether the app carries the M rating Australia now requires for paid chance-based purchases should be checked against the Australian rating record (Australian Classification Board, 2024), since a 2025 preprint found many top games wrongly classified (Carter et al., 2025).
Addiction / Harm Score: 5/10: Moderate. Documented mechanics:

Coin-staked matches. Players stake in-game currency on head-to-head matches (Apple, n.d.-a). The 2019 Children and Media Australia review reported that the starting currency ran out after a few short losses, after which players had to watch advertisements or buy more (Children and Media Australia, 2019).

Paid random draws. Surprise Boxes, scratchers and spins with published low-probability top prizes, a variable-reward structure of the kind examined in loot-box research (Miniclip, n.d.; Apple, n.d.-b).

Simulated-gambling side games (reported in 2019). The 2019 review described a spin wheel, Scratch and Win, boxes and a Hi-Lo guessing game, some requiring real money (Children and Media Australia, 2019); whether they remain in the current version was not confirmed.
Low, frequent price points. The US listing shows purchases from US$0.99 (Apple, n.d.-a).

Across 13 publications, the mean association between loot-box spending and problem gambling was r = .27 (Spicer et al., 2022), and a review of 64 outputs found reliable evidence linking loot boxes to problem gambling and gaming disorder, with only some evidence of financial harm (Greer et al., 2022). The score is lower than the social-casino apps because purchased in-game currency is not wagered on a casino game, and no cash-out route was discovered. This is a taxonomy assessment, not a clinical diagnosis.
4. Risk or Danger
Risk Level: Moderate: 5/10.
Chance-based purchases in a product open to teenagers. The 13+ US rating and loot-box label place paid random draws in front of young players.

Unofficial coin market and scams. Miniclip says the third-party coin sellers are not affiliated and cautions that users could face having their accounts banned or hacked, as well as losing payments (Miniclip Help and Support, n.d.). Resale value should be considered before finalising T2, because confirmed resale for real money would indicate T3.

Real-money pool variants alter risk exposure. Entry fees result in direct losses, and legality hinges on the skill-contest argument, which differs between jurisdictions. Cash competitions are not available in all areas, according to a commercial vendor, Skillz (Skillz, n.d.). This vendor statement has not been independently confirmed. The International Masters of Gaming Law (IMGL, 2026) reports that India’s 2025 Act does not distinguish between skill and chance in money games. The Australian position has not yet been established in this assessment and needs to be reviewed against the Interactive Gambling Act 2001 (Cth).
5. Tier Classification
Tier: T2: Paid Random Draw, No Cash-out (8 Ball Pool).
Classification path (8 Ball Pool):
8 Ball Pool → coins and cash bought or earned → coin-staked matches, Surprise Boxes, scratchers → virtual items and coins → no official cash-out route → T2
Path of Classification (skill-cash pool):
Skill contest pool application, cash entry fee, head-to-head/bracket competition, cash prize, and T4/T5 border.

Note for the taxonomy: 8 Ball Pool contrasts with the social-casino apps. Both spend purchased currency, but only the casino-style apps wager it on a chance game, which supports separating "paid random draw" from "stake on chance" as facets within T2.
6. Harm: Financial Harm and Psychological Harm
Financial Score: 5/10: Moderate

Financial harm. Loss is incremental, with small purchases accumulating over time. A review found some evidence linking loot-box purchasing to financial harm (Greer et al., 2022). Nothing in the sources reviewed puts a figure on pool-specific spending, so the financial score is an estimate.

Psychological harm. Time displacement, frustration and compulsive re-engagement are plausible pathways, but no peer-reviewed pool-specific research was found; the 2019 review is a consumer-advocacy assessment, not a study of harm outcomes (Children and Media Australia, 2019). The loot-box and problem-gambling association is the closest evidence (Spicer et al., 2022), and Langham et al. (2016) place emotional and psychological harm within their seven-category taxonomy of gambling-related harm.
7. Monetary Value
Monetary Value: Closed-loop virtual currency (no cash-out identified); real cash in and out for skill-cash variants
Cash-out pathways:
8 Ball Pool: none identified in official sources. Coins, cash and cues are usable only inside the game.
Unofficial market: third-party coin sellers exist (Miniclip Help and Support, n.d.). Whether coins or accounts can be resold by players for money is unverified.
Skill-cash pool: entry fee → prize pool → cash prize paid to winners (Skillz, n.d., vendor description).

Candidate Class

Primary Audience
Adults, including older adults. The Washington Attorney General alleges that children also play on parents' phones
Gambling Connection
High (simulated). Bingo is a chance game, and virtual currency bought with real money is staked on it; winnings are not cashable
Addiction / Harm Score
7/10: High
Risk Score
6/10: Moderate to High
Tier Classification
T2: paid random draw, no cash-out (Bingo Blitz). Bingo Cash: T4/T5 boundary
Financial Score
7/10: High
Monetary Value
Virtual currency bought with real money; winnings are credited as more virtual currency inside the app. Bingo Cash: cash entry fee in, cash prize out
Regulatory Status

Bingo Blitz: named in the Washington Attorney General's lawsuit (3 February 2026) alleging unlicensed gambling; these are allegations, and the case was still before the court in July 2026 (Washington State Office of the Attorney General, 2026; KOMO News, 2026). Australia requires R18+ for simulated gambling (Australian Classification Board, 2024). Bingo Cash: Papaya US$15M player class settlement with no admission of wrongdoing (ClassAction.org, 2025); a separate federal jury found in April 2026 that Papaya used undisclosed bots in games marketed as skill-based, and a US$719M judgment was entered in July 2026 (Perkins Coie, 2026; Takahashi, 2026).
1. Bingo

Bingo Blitz is a free-to-download bingo app published by Playtika. It is one of 16 casino-style apps named in the Washington Attorney General's 2026 lawsuit. It features a blue cartoon cat called Blitzy, a pink mouse called Moxie, a travel map with a photo album, and a linked YouTube channel (Washington State Office of the Attorney General, 2026). Bingo Cash is a separate real-money app from Papaya Gaming, which also makes Solitaire Cash, Bubble Cash, and 21 Cash (ClassAction.org, 2025).
2. Description and Connection to Gambling

Players buy virtual currency and use it to play bingo rounds for the chance of winning more virtual currency. The Washington State Attorney General's February 2026 lawsuit lists Bingo Blitz among 16 apps run by Playtika and Aristocrat and alleges that these are unlicensed gambling under Washington law and that the apps bank winnings inside the app, so the only way to use them is to keep playing (Washington State Office of the Attorney General, 2026). They are claims rather than established findings, and the characterisation of the games is disputed. One former chair of the Nevada Gaming Control Board said free-to-play apps that give no money or redeemable prize should be considered social entertainment (KOMO News, 2026).

Bingo Cash (Papaya Gaming) is a separate product using the same label. Players pay a fee to enter cash contests which are advertised as skill contests (ClassAction.org, 2025; Skillz, n.d., for the vendor’s description of the skill-contest model).

High (simulated) Gambling Connection: This is similar to gambling because people stake purchased currency on uncertain results. The difference from a casino is that the winnings are not paid out in cash.
3. Age Group and Addiction Risk

Primary age group: Adults, including older adults. A scoping review of gambling products and older adults (Johnson et al., 2023) revealed that the products themselves are virtually unstudied, while an ad-tech vendor’s glossary indicates that people over 50 typically spend the longest time playing social-casino games (adjoe, 2025; this is an industry claim, not independent research). The Washington complaint alleges that Bingo Blitz uses cartoon cats and children's-television-style content, that none of the 16 apps ask for a player's age, and that parents report children spending hundreds of dollars on their phones (Washington State Office of the Attorney General, 2026). Australian rules require simulated gambling to be classified R18+ (Australian Classification Board, 2024).
Addiction / Harm Score: 7/10: High. Documented or alleged mechanics:
Purchased currency staked on chance outcomes. Players buy virtual currency and wager it in rounds (Washington State Office of the Attorney General, 2026).
Winnings that stay in the app. As alleged, winnings are banked so the player's only use for them is further play (Washington State Office of the Attorney General, 2026).
Child-appealing presentation. Cartoon characters and a photo-album collection are alleged to be filled by playing bingo on a travel map (Washington State Office of the Attorney General, 2026).

Among at-risk gamblers who played social-casino games, greater frequency, variety, and spending were associated with more symptoms of problematic use (Gainsbury et al., 2017). The score is a taxonomy assessment, not a clinical diagnosis.
4. Risk or Danger
Risk Level: Moderate to High: 6/10.

Litigation and regulatory exposure. Washington's February 2026 suit follows a 2020 Playtika class-action settlement of US$38 million over claims under Washington law (Washington State Office of the Attorney General, 2026). The outcome of the 2026 case was not established in the sources reviewed.
Age-assurance gap (alleged). No age or date of birth is requested before play, and the 21-and-older term sits outside the app (Washington State Office of the Attorney General, 2026; KOMO News, 2026).

Deceptive contest design in Bingo Cash. Papaya agreed to a US$15 million settlement of claims that Bingo Cash, Solitaire Cash and other games used undisclosed bots in contests marketed as skill-based; the class covered deposits from 1 January 2019 to 5 September 2024, and the company did not admit wrongdoing (ClassAction.org, 2025). In the separate federal case brought by Skillz, a jury found in April 2026 that Papaya had used undisclosed bots in games marketed as fair and skill-based, and judgment was entered on 28 July 2026 (Perkins Coie, 2026; Regulatory Oversight, 2026): US$719 million in disgorgement in place of the jury's US$420 million, which Papaya may appeal (Takahashi, 2026). The sources consulted do not indicate the specific Papaya titles that the verdict refers to, so it is indicated here as evidence regarding Papaya’s practices in general.
5. Tier Classification
Tier: T2: Paid Random Draw, No Cash-out (Bingo Blitz).
Classification path (Bingo Blitz):
Bingo Blitz → virtual currency purchased using real money → bingo games based on chance → virtual currency won through play → no cash-out option → T2
Path to Classification (Bingo Cash):
Proceeds from the bingo entry fee go into a skill-contest bingo that pays out cash, with T4/T5 boundary proceeds going to Bingo Cash.

For the taxonomy: Both Bingo Blitz and Zynga Poker (Cards profile) have the same class and tier. They make a logical pair for the inter-rater exercise, as two coders should be able to classify them at the same tier based on the rule alone.
6. Harm: Financial Harm and Psychological Harm
Financial Score: 7/10: High

Financial harm. Since September 2020, Washington players are reported to have made over 8 million purchases on Playtika apps, spending over US$151 million. The Attorney General states that some individuals lost hundreds of thousands of dollars across the 16 apps (KOMO News, 2026; Washington State Office of the Attorney General, 2026). Because the winnings cannot be converted into cash, each purchase remains a cost to the player. Langham et al. (2016) categorise financial harm as one of seven types of harm.

Psychological harm. Playing to escape a negative mood is the most common symptom of problematic social-casino use, and greater psychological distress was linked to more severe problems (Gainsbury et al., 2017). When children access the app, their exposure to simulated gambling becomes a harm concern raised in the Washington complaint.
7. Monetary Value
Monetary Value: No cash out (closed-loop virtual currency) and Bingo Cash pays out cash prizes.
Cash-out pathways:
Bingo Blitz: money → virtual money → playing bingo → virtual currency that can be won. The complaint is for banked inside the app (Washington State Office of the Attorney General, 2026).
Bingo Cash: cash entry fee → contest → cash prize paid to winners (ClassAction.org, 2025).

Name

Candidate Class
Social-casino apps (free-to-play, purchasable chips), with real-money card variants at the far end of the cash-realisability scale
Primary Audience
Adults. The Google Play listing describes Zynga Poker as intended for adults; no age check was tested. Real-money variants target adult depositors
Gambling Connection
High. Social variants simulate poker with chance-driven chips and no cash-out; real-money variants are direct gambling or gambling-adjacent contests
Addiction / Harm Score
7/10: High
Risk Score
7/10: High
Tier Classification
T2: paid random draw, no cash-out (Zynga Poker). Real-money variants: T4/T5 boundary (skill-cash solitaire); T6 (unlicensed real-money poker in Australia, and online money games banned in India)
Financial Score
7/10: High
Monetary Value
Social variants: purchased chips, closed-loop, no cash-out route identified. Real-money variants: cash deposit in, cash prize or winnings out
Regulatory Status

Zynga Poker: no gambling licence identified; the App Store lists frequent simulated gambling (Apple, n.d.), and Australia requires R18+ for simulated gambling (Australian Classification Board, 2024; compliance not checked). Real-money variants: online money games are prohibited in India since 1 May 2026 (Lexology, 2026; Press Information Bureau, 2026), and the Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) has blocked unlicensed offshore poker sites (e.g. CoinPoker, June 2025; Gambling Insider, 2025). Papaya settled a US$15M player class action over alleged undisclosed bots without admitting wrongdoing (ClassAction.org, 2025); separately, a federal jury found in April 2026 that Papaya misrepresented its games as skill-based while using bots, and a US$719M judgment was entered in July 2026 (Perkins Coie, 2026; Takahashi, 2026).
1. Cards

"Cards" covers online games played with a standard deck, and it includes three kinds of products. Zynga Poker is a free-to-download Texas Hold'em app with tables, tournaments, a Challenge Pass, and a VIP programme (Apple, n.d.). Alongside it are skill-cash solitaire apps such as Papaya Gaming's Solitaire Cash, and real-money poker, rummy, and Teen Patti apps. Zynga Poker's core function is play, not payout, but the other two kinds take real money and pay real money out.
2. Description and Connection to Gambling

The three variants differ sharply in cash-realisability. Zynga Poker lets players wager virtual chips and buy random items (Apple, n.d.; Google, n.d.). Its Google Play listing describes it as intended for adults with no chance to win real money, while Apple labels it as containing frequent simulated gambling. Skill-cash solitaire, such as Solitaire Cash, requires cash deposits and offers contests with prizes that winners can withdraw (ClassAction.org, 2025). Skillz states that these contests should not be considered gambling because the results depend on skill instead of chance (Skillz, n.d.). However, this represents the platform’s own position rather than a decision made by a legal authority. Real-money poker, rummy, and Teen Patti apps are generally understood as gambling because participants stake funds for the possibility of receiving cash.

The gambling connection is thus a continuum, with the first variant as simulated, the second as contested, and the third as direct. In all three, there are chips or tokens in between the player and their money, and these are the loss-concealing mechanisms in the present study. According to a scoping review of experiments using monetary format, the evidence base is thin and inconsistent (Palmer et al., 2022), while pilot evidence suggests that players wager more with chips than with equivalent cash (Lapuz & Griffiths, 2010).
Gambling Connection: High (simulated to direct).
3. Age Group and Addiction Risk

Primary age group: Adults. Listings place Zynga Poker as an adult product. Although an age check was not tested within the app, a 2015 Australian review indicated that the simulated gambling was unsuitable for younger players (Children and Media Australia, 2015). Australia now has a rating of R18+ for simulated gambling and at least M for paid chance-based purchases (Australian Classification Board, 2024), although a 2025 preprint identified large proportions of top games given unsuitable ratings (Carter et al., 2025).
Addiction / Harm Score: 7/10: High. Documented mechanics:
Chip-based betting on outcomes involving chance. Poker hands are wagered in the form of chips that are purchased, won, or given as gifts, thus making it feel like the money is not being spent.

Free-chip bonuses. According to the App Store description, there is a very large welcome chip bonus and daily bonuses (Apple, n.d.), a form of temporal dark pattern described by Zagal et al. (2013) as encouraging return visits.
Progression passes and a VIP programme with respect to special chip packages (Apple, n.d.).
Random purchasable items. The listing reveals that some purchases provide chance-selected contents and refers players to in-game drop rates.

In one subsample of the survey, 176 adults who played social casino games and reported gambling problems showed that more frequent, more varied, and larger amounts spent on playing those games were linked to more symptoms of problematic use, with playing to escape a negative mood being the most prevalent symptom (Gainsbury et al., 2017). This is a taxonomy evaluation based on published studies and is not a clinical diagnosis.
4. Risk or Danger
Risk Level: High: 7/10.

Contests involving concealed automated opponents. Without admitting fault, a settlement of US$15M was announced by Papaya Gaming to settle a player class action lawsuit for allegedly running hidden bots in games such as Solitaire Cash while presenting them as skill-based contests (ClassAction.org, 2025). On 23 April 2026, a New York jury found that Papaya misrepresented its games as fair competitions between real players while using bots, and awarded US$420 million in damages (Perkins Coie, 2026). The court later substituted US$719 million in disgorgement for the jury’s award and added approximately US$10 million in fees when judgment was entered on 28 July 2026 (Regulatory Oversight, 2026). Papaya stated that it was considering an appeal (Takahashi, 2026). One law-firm commentary reports a higher overall total, so the court docket should be consulted before using the number. The settlement did not include findings, but the verdict did: a “skill” label does not mean that it is a fair contest.

Legal risk for online money games in India. The Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act 2025 bars online money games, including those that rely on skill or chance, such as real-money rummy and poker (International Masters of Gaming Law [IMGL], 2026; Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act 2025), and extends to services provided from abroad (Lexology, 2025).

Offshore real-money poker in Australia. The ACMA requested internet service providers to block unlicensed sites, such as the poker site CoinPoker in June 2025 (Gambling Insider, 2025), and has cautioned that illegal sites are unlikely to provide important consumer safeguards despite appearing legitimate (ACMA, 2024).
Zynga Poker itself sits at the low end of this group because no cash-out route exists. The higher risk score comes from the real-money variants that share the "cards" label.
5. Tier Classification
Tier: T2 for Zynga Poker; T4 to T6 for real-money variants.
Classification path (Zynga Poker):
Zynga Poker → purchased or free chips → chance-based card play and random items → chip balance → no cash-out route → T2
Classification path (skill-cash solitaire):
Solitaire Cash-style app → cash entry fee → skill contest → cash prize → T4/T5 boundary (paid and cashable, but a skill contest rather than licensed wagering)
Classification path (offshore poker, rummy, Teen Patti):
Real-money table → cash deposit → cash withdrawal → T6 in Australia (no Australian licence) and a prohibited online money game in India

Note for the taxonomy: "cards" is a game-type facet. The tier depends on the variant, and the skill-cash case needs a supervisor rule on whether it is T4 or T5. The bots theory in the federal case (Perkins Coie, 2026) is a further reason not to place skill-cash apps in T4 or T5 on the "skill" label alone.
6. Harm: Financial Harm and Psychological Harm
Financial Score: 7/10: High

Financial harm. In social variants, money spent on chips cannot be recovered, so each purchase is a pure cost. Real-money variants add direct loss of deposits, with no dispute route where the operator is unlicensed (ACMA, 2024). Langham et al. (2016) identify financial harm as one of seven categories of gambling-related harm and find that harm is not confined to people who meet diagnostic criteria.

Psychological harm. Playing to escape a negative mood is the leading reported symptom among at-risk social-casino players, and younger, less educated and more distressed gamblers reported greater problems (Gainsbury et al., 2017). That places emotional and psychological harm, another of Langham et al.'s (2016) categories, at the centre of this profile.
7. Monetary Value
Monetary Value: Closed-loop chips (social variant); real cash in and out (real-money variants)
Cash-out pathways:
Zynga Poker: money → chips → wagers → chip balance. No route to cash was identified in the store listings.
Skill-cash solitaire: cash deposit → cash contest → cash winnings paid to winners (ClassAction.org, 2025). Whether outcomes are genuinely skill-determined is contested (see Section 4).
Offshore poker, rummy and Teen Patti: deposit → real-money table → cash withdrawal at the operator's discretion, outside Australian or Indian consumer protection.

Taxonomy Factor
Classification
Name
Online casino (real-money): slots, roulette, blackjack, baccarat, live-dealer tables and crash games. Profiled as a class rather than a single brand
Candidate Class
Offshore/unlicensed bookmakers and casinos (T6 in Australia); licensed online casino (T5) in jurisdictions that license it
Primary Audience
Adults 18+ in principle. Unlicensed operators sit outside Australian consumer-protection rules, and lookalike branding is used to reach local players
Gambling Connection
Direct. Real money is staked on chance-based casino games with a cash payout
Addiction / Harm Score
9/10: Very High
Risk Score
8/10: High
Tier Classification
T6 in Australia (unlicensed and prohibited). T5 where the operator holds a recognised local licence
Financial Score
9/10: Very High
Monetary Value
Real cash deposited, converted to credits or chips and withdrawable as cash, subject to operator terms
Regulatory Status

Prohibited interactive gambling services are unlawful in Australia under the Interactive Gambling Act 2001 (Cth), and ACMA (2026) had blocked 1,788 illegal gambling and affiliate sites by August 2026. The service is lawful only where the operator holds a local licence.
1. Casino

Online casino websites and applications provide real-money casino games (slots, roulette, blackjack, baccarat, live-dealer tables and crash games). This profile does not consider them as a brand per se, but as a class. Unlike the retail or free-to-play apps from the previous profiles, their primary role is gambling.
2. Description and Connection to Gambling

Online casinos provide players with the ability to deposit money, then convert it to credits or chips, and play chance-based games like slots, roulette, blackjack, and live-dealer tables for a cash payout. These are interactive gambling services which are prohibited in Australia. The ACMA lists online casinos, online slot machines and in-play sports betting as prohibited, and the Interactive Gambling Act 2001 (Cth) is the operative law (ACMA, n.d.; Interactive Gambling Act 2001).

Enforcement involves issuing warnings and blocking websites. By August 2026, the ACMA had blocked 1,788 illegal gambling and affiliate sites, and more than 230 illegal services had withdrawn from the Australian market (ACMA, 2026). In 2025, ACMA’s warnings reached operators from Curaçao, the Netherlands and the Comoros (Public Gaming Research Institute, 2025). The chip-and-credit design that conceals the loss is behind the casino model, and pilot evidence indicates that gamblers bet larger amounts when they play with chips as opposed to comparable amounts of cash (Lapuz & Griffiths, 2010).
Gambling Connection: Direct. Real money is staked, and real money can be paid out.
3. Age Group and Addiction Risk

The primary age group for the profile will be adults (18+). There are some sites that do not have a licence and are not under Australian rules, and ACMA cautions that while these may appear legitimate, they are unlikely to have key consumer protections (ACMA, 2024). Lookalike brands, aggressive marketing, and the blocking of two imitation sites in November 2025 by the ACMA that posed as licensed Australian operators are what offshore operators are using (iGamingToday, 2025).

Addiction / Harm Score: 9/10 = Very High. The score is for direct cash at risk, round-the-clock access, and continuous-play games. It is higher than any social-casino profile, as a real monetary loss occurs after each round where you lose. Evidence on scale:

In 2011, a survey of a sample of online gamblers in Australia found that a large percentage of respondents were frequenting online gambling venues that were outside Australia, such as casino and poker websites, which the authors interpreted as evidence that the ban was not actually deterring online gambling. The sample was self-selected (Gainsbury et al., 2011).

Gainsbury (2014) quoted a government estimate that some 60% of Australian expenditure on interactive gambling was on prohibited gambling services overseas in 2010. The figure is outdated and should be treated only as an indication.

This is an assessment of a taxonomy, and not a clinical diagnosis. Both numbers are based on information over 10 years old and refer to offshore spending in general, not current spending on casino sites.
4. Risk or Danger
Risk Level: High: 8/10. Other jurisdictions' licensed operators are part of the class, which accounts for the lower score compared to Melbet's.
No recourse: The illegal operators are beyond Australian complaints and protection mechanisms, and even well-designed websites are unlikely to offer protections such as ACMA (ACMA, 2024).
Imitation sites. The sites have been blocked, despite claiming to be licensed Australian operators (iGamingToday, 2025).
Blocked sites reappear. It's a list of blocked sites that continues to grow as sites are blocked through enforcement. The reference point is the public list of blocked sites by the ACMA (n.d.).
A licence is not a form of protection. A licence from an offshore regulator is not an Australian licence and is not as stringent as the licences of stricter regulators (see Melbet's profile).
5. Tier Classification
Tier: T6 in Australia; T5 where licensed.
Classification path (Australia):
Online casino → cash deposit → chips or credits → real-money slots and tables → cash withdrawal → no Australian licence, prohibited service → T6
Classification path (licensed jurisdiction):
Same product → operator holds a recognised local licence → T5
Note for the taxonomy: the same product changes tier with jurisdiction. This is the strongest evidence for adding a jurisdiction facet to the game-and-role pair.
6. Harm: Financial Harm and Psychological Harm
Financial Score: 9/10: Very High

Financial harm. Deposits are lost to house edge in play, and where the operator is unlicensed a player who wins may face refused or delayed payment with no dispute route (ACMA, 2024). Langham et al. (2016) list financial harm first among seven categories, alongside relationship, emotional or psychological, health, work or study, criminal acts and cultural harm.

Psychological harm. Emotional and psychological harm is another of the seven categories, and Langham et al. (2016) found harm is not confined to people who meet diagnostic criteria. The same categories apply here, with the added stress of dealing with an operator outside any complaint scheme.
7. Monetary Value
Monetary Value: Real cash in, real cash out
Cash-out pathways:
Direct cash-out: deposit → chips or credits → play → withdrawal to the player's payment method, subject to the operator's terms and verification.
Regulatory status changes the pathway's reliability: licensed operators are subject to complaint processes, whereas unlicensed operators are not (ACMA, 2024).

Real cash (including INR, BDT and cryptocurrency) deposited and withdrawable, subject to operator terms
Regulatory Status

Claims a Curaçao licence (the number differs between sources and is unverified; see Section 2); no Australian licence. Online money games are prohibited in India under the 2025 Act, in force since 1 May 2026 (Lexology, 2026; Press Information Bureau, 2026); Bangladesh is described as a legal grey area (Football Whispers, 2026); an Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) site search for Melbet returned no results, which is weak evidence of non-blocking (ACMA, n.d.)
1. Melbet

Melbet is an international online bookmaker and casino, reported to have been founded in 2012. It offers sports betting including cricket and IPL markets, live betting, a casino of thousands of games and crash games such as Aviator, all under one account (Telecom Asia, n.d.; Football Whispers, 2026). Its core function is gambling, and the app is reported to be distributed as a direct download rather than through an app store (Football Whispers, 2026).
2. Description and Connection to Gambling

Review sites describe Melbet as operating in more than 100 countries, with 180-plus crash games such as Aviator among its casino offering (Telecom Asia, n.d.; Football Whispers, 2026). It is reported to accept UPI and Paytm in India, local payment systems in Bangladesh and cryptocurrency (Telecom Asia, n.d.; The Hans India, 2025; Goal.com India, 2026).

The operator claims a Curaçao licence, but sources give different licence numbers (8048/JAZ2020-060 in one review and OGL/2024/561/0554 in another) (Football Whispers, 2026; The Hans India, 2025). One review names the operating company as Pelican Entertainment B.V. and notes that a Curaçao licence gives weaker player protection than licences from regulators such as those of the UK, Malta, Sweden or Denmark (BetLuma, 2026). Another commercial source attributes the licence-number difference to Curaçao's licensing reform of 24 December 2024 (Allaxess, 2026); that explanation is itself unverified. Nearly all Melbet-specific sources are commercial review sites, some with affiliate links (BetLuma, 2026), so their statements are recorded as claims, not verified facts. Licensing, ownership, and payout claims are still to be independently verified by registration and regulatory notices and independent reporting by the Curaçao Gaming Authority.
Gambling Connection: Direct. Melbet is a real-money gambling site and covers the gambling sector of both sports and casino.
3. Age Group and Addiction Risk

Target age group: Adults who bet. Both the cricket and IPL markets and local payment methods suggest that the primary target market is South Asian bettors (Telecom Asia, n.d.; The Hans India, 2025). A broader audience is targeted through football, tennis, basketball, and kabaddi markets (Football Whispers, 2026).
Addiction / Harm Score: 9/10: Very High. The score will be increased if the following features are present:
Football Whispers (2026) and Telecom Asia, n.d. note that real money is available on all bets, with live betting and crash games offering the possibility of quick betting again.
Very large casino library, with more than 5,000 games under one account, and also offering sports betting (Telecom Asia, n.d.).
This is a taxonomy assessment drawing on published research on gambling harm (Langham et al., 2016), not a clinical diagnosis.
4. Risk or Danger
Risk Level: Very High: 9/10.

Legal status in India. The Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act 2025 bans online money games (both skill-based and chance-based), extends to services operated outside of India and prohibits their advertising (Lexology, 2025; International Masters of Gaming Law [IMGL], 2026; Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act 2025). Goal.com India (2026) describes Melbet as safe for Indian players because it is offshore, but that claim conflicts with the reach of this Act and should not be repeated without consulting a lawyer. The Act and its Rules entered into force on 1 May 2026 but, according to the Press Information Bureau (2026) and Lexology (2026), a judicial challenge against the Act was reported to be pending.

Legal status elsewhere. According to one review, Bangladesh can be described as a legal grey area with regard to offshore betting (Football Whispers, 2026). A real-money wagering service is unlicensed if it does not have an Australian licence under the project’s tier rule. When searching for Melbet on the ACMA site, no results appeared, but this does not necessarily mean that it is not blocked, as the site search is not the blocked-sites register, so the absence is weak evidence and the register should be consulted directly (ACMA, n.d.).

Withdrawal disputes (unverified). Melbet pages on Trustpilot show reviews alleging delayed and refused withdrawals, alongside Melbet’s responses asking the reviewers to reach out to support and positive reviews (Trustpilot, 2026a, 2026b). The www.melbet.com page has been given a Trustpilot integrity warning (rating withheld after fake reviews have been deleted), which means that the reviews on the page cannot be relied upon either way. These are not findings, but allegations made by users.
The Android version of the app is downloaded directly from the operator's website in APK file format, avoiding app stores, according to a review from Football Whispers (2026).
5. Tier Classification
Tier: T6: Unlicensed or Offshore Real-money Wagering.
Classification path:

Melbet → local-payment or crypto deposit → sports bets and casino games → cash withdrawal (bank, e-wallet, crypto) → offshore operator with no Australian licence; prohibited online money game in India → T6

Note for the taxonomy: Melbet is an offshore bookmaker, a cricket wagering platform, and an online casino. A clear example of the need for the taxonomy to be faceted, not hierarchical, and why a claimed licence should not, in isolation, move an operator from T6 to T5.
6. Harm: Financial Harm and Psychological Harm
Financial Score: 9/10: Very High

Financial harm. Losses are actual cash, and if the operator is offshore, then a player does not have an Australian or Indian complaint mechanism (ACMA, 2024, for Australian illegal operators). Withdrawals are said to not be processed or are being refused (Trustpilot, 2026a, 2026b), but this is not verified. Cryptocurrency payment methods are disclosed (Goal.com India, 2026); It is generally difficult to reverse a crypto payment. As part of the seven harm categories, financial harm is identified by Langham et al. (2016).

Psychological harm. There was no evidence specific to Melbet about psychological harm. Emotional and psychological harm are included in a seven-category taxonomy of gambling-related harm outlined by Langham et al. (2016), and relationship, health, work or study harm, and harm from criminal acts are identified. The latter applies in the context of the present issue, as participation in a banned money game is legally liable in India.
7. Monetary Value
Monetary Value - Real Cash in, Real Cash out (bank, e-wallet, cryptocurrency)
Cash-out pathways:

Payment methods that have been reported to have been used include bank transfers, e-wallets like Skrill, and cryptocurrency (Goal.com India, 2026); UPI and Paytm in India (Telecom Asia, n.d.); and local Bangladeshi systems with a reported minimum withdrawal of 500 BDT and a stated maximum processing time of 24 hours (The Hans India, 2025).

Fast payment is a claim made by review sites which is countered by user allegations of delays, contesting the reliability of the pathway (Trustpilot, 2026a, 2026b). The tier does not indicate that cash comes out reliably; it indicates that cash, in theory, can come out.
